predecessors.name: Later Jin dynasty
predecessors.text: the Later Jin / Qing realm of 1644 in Manchuria, Inner Mongolia and Liaoxi

predecessors.name: Ming dynasty
predecessors.text: Beijing and North China, the part of the Ming shape that the Qing 1645 shape covers

successors.name: Republic of China
successors.text: China proper, Manchuria, Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang

successors.name: Great Mongol State (Bogd Khanate of Mongolia)

ledger.x: 1644: the court moves from Shenyang to Beijing.
1644: Korea (Joseon) is a Qing tributary.
1644: the Qing enter Beijing and begin to rule China from there.
1644: Beijing and North China pass to the Qing.
1644: the Qing hold Hebei and Shandong.
1645: the Qing take Nanjing, the Hongguang court's capital.
1645: Hangzhou falls.
By 1646: Gansu is under Qing rule.
ledger.cp: Ming remnants and local powers in Gansu (no dossier)

ledger.x: February 1646: the Qing take Zhejiang west of the Qiantang.

17 October 1646: Fuzhou falls and Fujian passes to the Qing. after 'the fall of Fuzhou on 17 October' Zheng Zhilong defected; the Longwu Emperor was 'summarily executed in Tingzhou'; Koxinga went on resisting from the coast.
20 January 1647: Guangzhou is taken.
1648: Sichuan is Qing land in Cliopatria's 1648 shape (71 percent of the province).
ledger.cp: Zhang Xianzhong's Xi regime and Ming loyalists in Sichuan

ledger.x: 1649-50: the Qing reconquer the middle south.
24 November 1650: Guangzhou falls again.
August 1652: Li Dingguo retakes Guilin.
1659: Guizhou and Guangxi are Qing land again in Cliopatria's 1659 shape (100 percent of each).
January 1659: Kunming falls and the last Southern Ming emperor flees to Burma.
December 1673: Wu Sangui revolts in the south-west.
1674: Wu Sangui's forces hold Hunan and Sichuan.
1674: Geng Jingzhong rises in Fujian.
1674: Sun Yanling rises in Guangxi (and Wang Fuchen in Shaanxi).
1676: Shang Zhixin joins the revolt.
1678: Qing forces retake the Hunan strongholds.
1680: four provinces recovered.
1680: Fujian and Guangdong are back.
December 1681: the Three Feudatories revolt ends at Kunming.
October 1683: Taiwan surrenders to the Qing.
1685: the Qing drive the Russians from the Amur.
27 August 1689: the Treaty of Nerchinsk ends the fighting on the Amur.
27 August 1689: the Qing hold the Amur basin to the Stanovoy Range.
September 1690: Qing and Dzungar armies fight at Ulan Butong.
1691: the Khalkha princes submit to the Qing at Dolon Nor.
1696: the Khalkha vassalage becomes incorporation.
May 1696: Galdan is crushed at Jao Modo (Zuunmod).
1696: Outer Mongolia passes from the Dzungars to the Qing.
1720: the Qing expel the Dzungars from Tibet and set up a protectorate.
1724: Amdo becomes the Qing province of Qinghai.
1726-27: eastern Kham is annexed to Sichuan.
1731: Qing and Dzungars fight on the western Mongolian frontier.
1739: the Qing-Dzungar border is fixed by treaty.
1755: the Qing army enters Ili.
1757: the Zunghars are defeated.
1757: Dzungaria becomes Qing land.
1757: the Kumul Khanate (Hami) is incorporated as a vassal.
1759: the Tarim Basin completes the conquest of Xinjiang.
1791: the Gorkhas occupy Shigatse.
1792: the Gorkhas are driven back.
1803: Vietnam under the Nguyen is a Qing tributary.
1842: Hong Kong Island is ceded to Britain.
19 March 1853: the Taiping take Nanjing and make it their Heavenly Capital.
1856: the Panthay Rebellion takes western Yunnan.
28 May 1858: the Treaty of Aigun: the Amur's left bank to Russia, the Ussuri country a joint zone.
1858: Jiujiang and the rest of Jiangxi are retaken.
March 1860: the Taiping take Hangzhou, then Changzhou and Suzhou.
October 1860: the Convention of Peking.
14 November 1860: the Russo-Chinese Convention of Peking settles the Ussuri country.
14 November 1860: Outer Manchuria goes to Russia.
1861: Zeng Guofan takes Anqing.
December 1861: the Taiping take Ningbo and hold Zhejiang.
10 May 1862: Ningbo is reclaimed.
June 1862: the Hui rise in Shaanxi.
October 1863: the Hui take Ningxia.
June 1864: the Tarim rises.
July 1864: Nanjing falls to the imperial armies and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom ends.
Summer to autumn 1864: the rebels take Dzungaria.
ledger.cp: Dungan and Taranchi rebels of Dzungaria (no dossier)

ledger.x: 3 October 1864: the Urumqi fortress falls.
1865: Yaqub Beg takes Kashgar.
3 March 1866: Qing rule in the Ili Valley ends.
1869: the Hui are cleared from Shaanxi.
1871: Russia occupies the Ili Valley.
January 1871: Ma Hualong surrenders at Jinjibao.
Late 1872: Xining falls.
1873: the Panthay Rebellion ends and Yunnan is whole.
24 October 1873: Suzhou (Jiuquan) falls to Zuo Zongtang's siege guns, securing the Hexi Corridor.
August 1876: the Qing retake Urumqi and Dzungaria.
18 December 1877: the Qing enter Kashgar and Yettishar ends.
1881: Russia returns the Ili region.
1885: the Treaty of Tientsin ends Chinese suzerainty over Vietnam.
17 April 1895: the Qing lose Korea.
17 April 1895: Taiwan is ceded to Japan.
1898: Germany leases Jiaozhou Bay.
1898: Russia leases Liaodong.
1898: Britain leases the New Territories.
1898: France leases Guangzhouwan.
29 June 1900: Russia invades Manchuria.
1905: the Russian occupation of Manchuria ends in Cliopatria's shape.
February 1910: Qing troops enter Lhasa.
1911: Outer Mongolia leaves the Qing.
ledger.cpn: Great Mongol State (Bogd Khanate of Mongolia)

ledger.x: 1912: the Qing garrison at Lhasa surrenders.
1912: Tibet's tie to the Qing ends with the dynasty.
1912: the Kumul Khanate passes to the Republic.
1912: the lease of Jiaozhou Bay outlives the dynasty and passes to the Republic (the end here is the Qing's, not the lease's).
1912: the Kwantung lease outlives the dynasty (the end here is the Qing's, not the lease's).
1912: the lease of the New Territories outlives the dynasty and passes to the Republic (the end here is the Qing's, not the lease's).
1912: the lease of Guangzhouwan outlives the dynasty and passes to the Republic (the end here is the Qing's, not the lease's).
12 February 1912: the last emperor abdicates and the Qing ends.

wars.name: Qing conquest of the Ming
wars.outcome: Qing victory: Beijing and North China in 1644, Nanjing in June 1645, Fuzhou on 17 October 1646, Guangzhou in 1647 and 1650, Yunnan in January 1659; the Yongli Emperor was executed in 1662.

wars.name: Revolt of the Three Feudatories
wars.outcome: Qing victory after eight years: Hunan retaken 1678, four provinces in 1680, Kunming in October 1681, the rebels surrender in December 1681; 'By 1681, the Qing government had established control over a ravaged southern China' (Qing dynasty page).

wars.name: Battle of Penghu
wars.outcome: Qing victory: Tungning was 'defeated in 1683 at the Battle of Penghu' by Shi Lang; Zheng Keshuang surrendered in October 1683 and Taiwan became Qing land.

wars.name: Sino-Russian border conflicts
wars.outcome: Qing victory at Albazin (1685, 1686) and the Treaty of Nerchinsk of 27 August 1689: the Qing hold the Amur basin to the Stanovoy Range, Russia the Argun-Baikal country; the border west of the Argun was fixed at Kyakhta in 1727.

wars.name: Dzungar–Qing Wars
wars.outcome: Qing victory: the Khalkha submit at Dolon Nor (1691), Galdan is crushed at Jao Modo (May 1696), the Dzungars are expelled from Tibet (1720), the border is fixed by a treaty (1739), Dzungaria is added after the 1755-1758 campaigns and the Dzungar population…

wars.name: Sino-Nepalese War
wars.outcome: Qing and Tibetan victory: the Gorkhas, who sacked Tashilhunpo in 1791, were pursued to the Kathmandu Valley and 'Nepal conceded defeat'; no land changed hands.

wars.name: First Opium War
wars.outcome: British victory: the Treaty of Nanjing (1842) opened treaty ports and ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain.

wars.name: Taiping Rebellion
wars.outcome: Qing victory: Nanjing fell to the imperial armies in July 1864; Hong Xiuquan had died in June; the last Taiping army was destroyed in August 1871.

wars.name: Nian Rebellion
wars.outcome: Suppressed by 1868 (Zuo defeated the Nian rebels by 1868, Dungan Revolt page).

wars.name: Panthay Rebellion
wars.outcome: Qing victory in 1873; Yunnan whole again.

wars.name: Second Opium War
wars.outcome: Anglo-French victory: the Arrow incident of 1856, the Treaty of Tientsin signed in 1858 and ratified in 1859, Beijing captured in 1860 and the Convention of Beijing signed by Prince Gong; the Kowloon cession is not on the pages opened (ledger, confidence 1).

wars.name: Amur Annexation
wars.outcome: Russian gain without a Russo-Chinese war: the Treaty of Aigun (28 May 1858) and the Convention of Peking (14 November 1860) gave Russia 'all land north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri', about 910,000 km2.

wars.name: Dungan Revolt (1862–1877)
wars.outcome: Qing victory under Zuo Zongtang: Shaanxi cleared by 1869, Jinjibao in January 1871, Xining in late 1872, Suzhou in October 1873, Kashgar on 18 December 1877; the Ili region returned by Russia in 1881.

wars.name: Sino-French War
wars.outcome: The war ended with the Treaty of Tientsin (1885), which recognised the French protectorate in Vietnam; the Qing lose their suzerainty over Vietnam, no Qing land changes hands.

wars.name: First Sino-Japanese War
wars.outcome: Japanese victory: the Treaty of Shimonoseki (17 April 1895) ceded Taiwan and the Penghu Islands, ended the Qing suzerainty over Korea and ceded Liaodong, which was 'returned by the Triple Intervention'.

wars.name: Boxer Rebellion
wars.outcome: The Eight-Nation Alliance invaded and the Boxer Protocol followed; Cixi fled to Xi'an in 1900.

wars.name: Russian invasion of Manchuria
wars.outcome: Russian victory in the field, with Manchuria 'partially' and later 'mostly' occupied; Russia did not annex it ('His Majesty decided not to annex any part of China').

wars.name: Xinhai Revolution
wars.outcome: The Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 set off the revolt of 14 of the 22 provinces by November; the Republic of China was created at Nanjing on 1 January 1912; Puyi abdicated on 12 February 1912.

certainty.note: The conquest of the south is provincial lines, the rebel zones of 1673-81 move yearly, and the Russian and Mongolian frontiers are undefined until Nerchinsk (1689).
Sharp lines: the Amur-Stanovoy line from the Treaty of Nerchinsk (27 August 1689), and the 1726 Lhasa-Beijing boundary in Kham (stone monument).
Sharp: the Amur-Ussuri frontier (Convention of Peking, 14 November 1860), the coast and the 1898 leases.
